title: Chief economists see both big AI data-centre benefits and ‘significant’ local pushback yet to come
gist: In the WEF's September 2026 Chief Economists' Outlook, 79% of respondents expect significant local pushback against AI data centres in the year ahead, while 78% expect data-centre investment to drive a significant share of global growth and nearly 7 in 10 expect meaningful AI productivity gains. The same economists doubt the jobs payoff (61% say no significant job-creation share). Resistance is driven by electricity, water and tax-break concerns, from US states and Gary, Indiana's one-year moratorium to Ireland, Brazil, Chile and Australia. EY's Gregory Daco frames the backlash as the usual capital-intensive first phase of a technology revolution.

themes.theme: Economists' split verdict: growth yes, jobs no

insights.claim: 79% of chief economists surveyed in the WEF's September 2026 Chief Economists' Outlook expect significant local community pushback against AI data-centre expansion in the year ahead. That puts it close to their confidence that food costs will rise (88%) and that geopolitical conflict will remain a source of uncertainty (97%).
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Mainstream economists now treat local opposition to data centres as a near-consensus macro risk. Price permitting and siting delays into hyperscaler capex timelines and data-centre REIT and developer pipelines.
insights.quote: 79% of respondents in the latest Chief Economists’ Outlook expect meaningful local resistance to artificial-intelligence data centres in the year ahead.
insights.locator: Opening summary / Chief Economists' Outlook survey results

insights.claim: 78% of surveyed chief economists expect data-centre investment to drive a significant share of global economic growth in the year ahead. That is almost the same share that expects local pushback, so economists see data centres as a major growth engine and a major friction point at once.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Global growth is concentrated in AI capex. A capex slowdown caused by local resistance would hit GDP directly, not only tech earnings.
insights.locator: Nearly the same percentage of chief economists

insights.claim: Nearly seven in ten surveyed chief economists expect AI adoption to deliver meaningful productivity gains within the next 12 months.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Economists now expect near-term AI productivity gains. If those gains don't show up in 2026-27 productivity data, the growth case for continued data-centre capex weakens.
insights.locator: If productivity is essential for healthy growth

insights.claim: 61% of surveyed chief economists do not expect data-centre investment to drive a significant share of global job creation in the year ahead. Estimates cited in the article put a single data centre's direct permanent workforce at only a few dozen to a few hundred employees.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Data centres bring high capex but few jobs, which weakens the local political case built on employment and makes community approval harder to secure. Expect more scrutiny of tax incentives.
insights.quote: 61% of them do not expect data centre investment to drive a significant share of global job creation in the year ahead.

insights.claim: EY's Gregory Daco says the AI build-out is the first phase of a technological revolution, which is always capital-intensive. That phase historically strains resources and so triggers pushback, as it did in the Industrial Revolution, the electricity revolution and the computer age.
insights.speaker: Gregory Daco
insights.so_what: Under this view, backlash comes with capex intensity, so local opposition should ease as the build-out shifts from constructing infrastructure to deploying and using it.
insights.quote: What we are currently seeing is the first phase of any technological revolution
insights.locator: Radio Davos remarks by Gregory Daco

insights.claim: Past technology booms drew fierce public opposition that did not stop the technology. The railroad boom of the Industrial Revolution provoked backlash, 19th-century electrification caused public unease and labour unrest, and the early computer age saw a wave of mainframe sabotage. The article argues economies ultimately benefited each time, though the adjustment was rough.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Historical precedent suggests backlash delays and reshapes infrastructure booms but rarely reverses them. Treat opposition as a timing and cost risk, not an existential one.
insights.quote: The adjustment process was not always pretty.
insights.locator: A railroad-building boom during the Industrial Revolution

insights.claim: Gregory Daco of EY expects the AI boom to have mixed effects, while the article calls data-centre disillusionment a 'rare hiccup' in AI's otherwise relentless advance. Both argue for closer collaboration between governments and private companies on data centres.
insights.speaker: Gregory Daco
insights.so_what: Expect public-private deals (community benefit agreements, grid co-investment, heat reuse) to become standard for permitting. Developers that can offer them gain a siting advantage.
insights.quote: It's not necessarily going to be all good or all bad
insights.locator: Their environmental footprint is a work in progress

insights.claim: Several US states are rethinking tax exemptions they granted to attract data-centre construction, because the facilities consume huge amounts of electricity and water.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Withdrawn state tax incentives would directly raise data-centre project costs. Track state legislative sessions for sales-tax exemption rollbacks that affect hyperscaler and colocation economics.
insights.locator: Here's what they have seen, so far

insights.claim: In Europe, opponents have targeted data-centre projects in Austria, France, Italy and Ireland. In Ireland, data centres used about a fifth of all electricity by 2024.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Ireland shows how grid saturation turns into political constraint. Markets where data centres approach double-digit shares of power demand face the highest risk of moratoria or connection limits.
insights.quote: a country where data centres accounted for about a fifth of all electricity usage by 2024
insights.locator: In Europe, opponents have targeted projects

insights.claim: In Latin America, Indigenous people protested construction of Brazil's biggest data centre, and a Chilean activist complained that data centres are being prioritized over the population.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Emerging-market data-centre hubs marketed as cheap-power and cheap-land alternatives carry social-licence risk, especially over water, which could delay projects.
insights.quote: data centres are being given priority over the population
insights.locator: In Latin America, Indigenous people protested

insights.claim: An Australian non-profit warned that wholesale electricity prices in the country's most populous state could rise 26% if growing data-centre demand is not met with renewable energy.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Data-centre load can move wholesale power prices by double digits. This supports generators and renewables developers, and it is also why regulators may make data-centre connections conditional on supplying their own clean power.

themes.theme: Scale of the build-out and its resource footprint

insights.claim: The US has more than 5,000 data centres at some stage of development, about ten times more than any other country, according to research cited in the article. Germany follows with 529, the UK with 523 and China with 449.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The US hosts about 10x more data centres than any other country, so both AI capex upside and local-backlash risk are concentrated in US jurisdictions. US state and municipal politics are the key variable.

insights.claim: By late 2025, data centres worldwide were consuming enough energy to power New York state at peak demand, according to research cited in the article. Their annual cooling-water use may exceed the drinking-water needs of 1.2 million people.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Power and water are the binding constraints and the main political flashpoints. This supports utilities, grid equipment makers and water-efficient cooling technology.
insights.locator: Globally, the facilities were consuming enough energy

insights.claim: Data-centre operators are responding to environmental criticism by cooling with seawater, running on renewable electricity and putting their waste heat to other uses. The article says their environmental footprint remains a work in progress.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Mitigation technology (alternative cooling, heat reuse, on-site renewables) is increasingly needed to get projects permitted. That creates demand for vendors in those niches.
insights.locator: Their environmental footprint is a work in progress

themes.theme: Gary, Indiana: moratorium despite jobs promise

insights.claim: Gary, Indiana has income per person about half the US average and a poverty rate three times higher. Concerns there that AI data centres would raise electricity bills for an already struggling community led the mayor to impose a one-year moratorium on new data-centre facilities within city limits, even though Gary has no data centres yet.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Pass-through of power costs to households is now the key political trigger. Municipal moratoria can appear before any facility exists, so screen pipeline sites for exposure to residential rate increases.
insights.quote: Last week, Gary's mayor established a one-year moratorium on new data centre facilities.
insights.locator: Gary, Indiana doesn't actually have any data centres

insights.claim: A recent study found that building a particularly large data centre in the northwest Indiana region that includes Gary could create nearly 3,000 jobs per year, counting external support roles. Local government still blocked new facilities within city limits for now, which shows that promised jobs are not overcoming opposition over power costs.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Job-creation pitches, which rely mostly on indirect roles, are losing political force. Developers may need to offer direct rate protection or community payments to win approvals.
